variants.text: She's the Godspeed Ginny. Somebody named her that. Four knots. Downhill. With a tailwind.
Godspeed Ginny. The name was optimistic and the boat has never once agreed with it.
Yes, Godspeed. No, I don't know who. Whoever it was never met her.
That BREEZY showing through the transom? Previous owner. Lovely man. Bit of a windbag.
You've spotted BREEZY under the paint. That was a horse. If I told you the story, you'd have a long face too.
BREEZY. The paint's coming off. The name isn't. That's loyalty, or poor paint.
Ahead of you — KNIGHT FALLS. Forty-two cubits of thundering water. And another three that are quiet.
Forty-two cubits, folks. I'm required to say it. I've never been told what a cubit is.
Forty-two cubits. That's the figure in the brochure. I use my brochure as an umbrella.
variants.follow: Water comes over the rail and over everyone's head and, yes, behind the brochure.

variants.text: Knight Falls. Named after Sir Knight. *Looks at the chart.* Oh, sorry. Sir Dwight.
No. Don't jump. NOT THAT KIND OF BAIL.
THE BUCKET. SIR. The bucket. Sit down.
I said bail. I meant the buckets. We have been over this.
Two ducks, one either side. Steer between them and you create a para-ducks.
Duck to port, duck to starboard. Straight up the middle and we've got ourselves a para-ducks.
Duck… duck… GOOSE.
Two ducks and a— that's a goose. That's a goose, folks.
Duck. Duck. … grey duck?
I had shares in that mine. Of all the things I've lost in my life, it's my mine I miss the most.
Shares. In that. Bought high. Sold low. My finances really went down the shaft after that.
I'm really expecting good things from this trip. The last time I had a sinking feeling about a trip was when I worked for the White Star Line.
I served on the poop deck. …It's a real term. It's from the French. La poupe. It's in the— stop laughing. That job stunk.
Poop deck. Raised deck aft. Nautical term, centuries old. My boss' name was John. And yes. That job stunk.
My first posting was the poop deck. I'd thank you not to make it a thing. This was my #2 joke! It stunk.
Off the port bow — the Calliope. Aground since '13. Same chart, same fork, same wide water and good bottom. That, folks, is a steaming pile.
She was the pride of the upper river. Now she's a steaming pile. And I do mean steaming. Boiler's still going. Nobody's told it.
That's the competition. Sorry — that WAS the competition. Steam launch, hard aground, listing. A steaming pile.

title: He read the same three words

variants.text: Same chart as mine. Same fork. He read the same three words I read. I just read them slower.
There's no version of this where I'm better than him. There's only a version where I was slower that day.
Reverse is more of a suggestion on this boat. So whatever's ahead — we're going in,,,over,,,under,,through,,,.
She doesn't back up. She's never backed up. We commit, or we discuss it with the bank.
Safety valve's painted shut. Pressure only goes one way. Good news — the fix is more speed.
When she starts screaming, we go faster. I know. I've stopped arguing with it.
Chart calls this stretch wide water, good bottom. Named after someone the surveyor met that season. …I hear it. I hear it now.
'Wide water, good bottom,' it says. In his handwriting. Named for a personal acquaintance. *Looks hard at the chart* Does it say Sandy?
Hippopotamus. Four tons, opens to a hundred and fifty degrees. That's not a yawn, that's an appointment.
They look sleepy. It's a trick. The napping is how they scout.
They say there are crocodiles. I think it's a croc.
You were promised crocodiles. I was promised a quiet bend. I think we both got a croc.
Home port's Cra-Zi. Spelled on the chart the way a drunk surveyor heard it. If you pronounce it any other way, you're crazy.
Cra-Zi. Two syllables, one hyphen, zero relation to what the locals actually call it.
That sign says NOWHERE — THREE DAYS. My love life is going there- fast.
You want to go to Nowhere? Everyone does. It's three days. It's always three days.
The crate? Cargo. Nothing to— the telegram said LEOPARD SPOTTED. Then SPOTTED LEOPARD. I never got a clarification.
Don't put fingers through the slats. That's not a rule, that's a eulogy.
That's the piano. It does that every wake. It's been doing it for nine miles. It's in the key of wet.
Yes, the freight is playing. No, I can't stop it. That is its forte.
Madam, that's the hospital's ice. You're melting it. Slowly, but with commitment.
The ice is for the hospital. It is not a bench. Ma'am. It is not a bench.
The river's called the Unnamed. That's not me being coy. He left the box blank and the printer set it in capitals.
You're on the Unnamed River. Named, in the end, by a man who couldn't be bothered to ask.
The Unnamed. Yes. I know. No, there isn't another one.
This water's been called the Unnamed, Sin Nombre, Rio Sem Nome, Sans Nom, and Innominata. Five languages.
Every outfit that came through wrote down 'unnamed' and thought they were copying the last lot.
Innominata's on the oldest sheet, so that's the one the lawyers use. It means the same as all the others.
Some charts say Nonesuch. That's a clerk who read 'no such name' and thought it was pretty.
The Nonesuch. Sounds grand. It's a filing error with good handwriting.
The people who live here have always had a name for the river. It's never been on a chart. Wait. The chart says Sigismund. S-M-I-T-H. Would you look at that!
The people on this bank have always had a name for the river. Never written down. Wait. The chart says Ghislain. S-M-I-T-H. Would you look at that!
Every wrong name on this water could be corrected tomorrow. It would cost money, but all my assets are liquid.
Every boat on this river runs the same chart. One survey. One season. One man with a flask and a bad ear.
This chart's wrong in the same places for everybody. Comforting, in a way.
I'm not, strictly speaking, licensed. I mention it early so it isn't a surprise later.
Licensing is a complicated subject on this river and I'd rather we enjoyed the trees. My ex-wife said I was simple.
DUCK! …the branch. THE BRANCH. Not the birds. Why are you looking at the birds.
Everybody DUCK — no, down. DOWN. Sir, there are no ducks here.
Safety briefing: the boat floats. That's the whole briefing. Please hold us to it.
Rule one: stay in the boat. Rule two: see rule one. If your feet are wet, make sure they are in the boat.
Tips are welcome. Refunds are handled by a clerk in Cra-Zi named Dennis, whom I've never met and suspect is a ledger.
Gratuities are optional. Complaints are mandatory, and Dennis reads every one. Dennis has a round opening.
Everything on this cruise is complimentary. That includes the leaks.
Complimentary water is available throughout. Throughout the boat. Mind your shoes.
The brochure said 'leisurely.' It didn't say whose.
The brochure promised 'an unhurried voyage.' Nobody consulted the boiler.
This hat came with the boat. I was told it was the last skipper's. And that it was pulled out of the river.
I've worn this hat for eleven years. It's the only thing aboard that's never let me down, and that is not a compliment to the hat.
One blast on the whistle means hello. Two means brace. Three means I've said something I regret.
The whistle has three settings: polite, urgent, and apology.
Wave to the bank, folks. Nobody's waved at it all week. It'll tell its friends.
Go on, wave. The bank is very shy. It's been that way since the bridge.
First day on the river, I made a rule: never look surprised. I haven't looked surprised since. I've been very, very surprised.
I've never once been surprised on this river. I've only been caught holding the same expression.
People say Ginny's on her last legs. She's never had a first one.
If a bolt lets go, leave it. She's decided to travel lighter and I don't argue with the hull.
The story of how the boat was put together? It's riveting.
The compass points north. *Taps the compass* Maybe not,,,,.
Compass says north. River says 'we'll see.' I tend to side with the river; it's bigger.
Photographs are welcome. Flash is discouraged. Make sure you get the river's good side.
No flash, please. Last time, the river saw how it looked and felt drained. Three boats were stranded.
Let's have a moment of silence for the previous skipper. …There. He'd have hated that. He loved noise.
A moment's silence for the last skipper, who retired in a hurry. Me? I'm just tired.
Please remain seated. Anyone standing will be mistaken for a mast, and I'll steer by you.
Remain seated, please. The boat is happier, and so, in a small way, am I.
This is the kind of trip you'll tell your grandchildren about. Not because it was good. Because they'll ask where your shoes went.
You'll tell this story at dinners for years. Leave out the middle. Everyone does.
I hold a master's licence. I think it is in fishing or bait or something.
My credentials hang on the wall of my office in Cra-Zi. It says 'Wanted.'
If you're under ten, you're in charge of your own parents.
Junior crew, I have a job for you: watch for trouble. If you see any, point at it and say nothing. It's what I do.
What does that sign say? It says 'Cra-Zi. Population forty, if the sign is honest.' Count heads on the landing. ... Stop at thirty. The sign gets sensitive.
Welcome to Cra-Zi. Founded, burned, rebuilt, still burning and rebuilding. We take pride in our consistency.
That pier. 1820. If we make it back, it'll say 1821.
You in the sensible shoes. They'll be sensibly wet later.
Set your watches by the landing clock. ... Now put them away. Half past never is close enough for this river.
The clock is right twice a day. My boss? Never.
Last look at Cra-Zi. Take a photograph. By the time we're back, half of it will have been rebuilt and the other half will be on fire.
Last look at the landing. Count the windows. If the number changes, we are in the wrong town.
Wet feet are included. The river added them to the ticket.
Ankles is a greeting. Knees is a meeting. We are at ankles. Bail if we adjourn.
Who was Ginny? Nobody asks. Everybody wonders. It's the one mystery on this river I'm paid to keep.
Ginny. Lovely name. Nobody's told me who she was, and I've learned not to push.
I was told Ginny is the boss's college roommate's adopted third cousin, estranged on her mother's side. What does that mean? Nothing. Absolutely nothing.
Two horsepower. I met one. He was lying down and a vet was checking him out.
She's rated at two horsepower. One is the engine. The other is hope.
Ma'am, you are in charge of the anchor if we need it. What? It's painted on? Makes your job easy then.
We used to carry an anchor for morale. Morale's been at the bottom ever since.
The life belt's instructions are printed on the life belt. Please read them now. It's harder when it's wet.
You. The hat. Trade it for the cork one. The hat has plans that do not include floating.
We carry a full crew: one skipper, one boiler, and a boy who left in March.
Crew complement is me. We keelhauled the rest. What a drag on morale.
That noise has been going since Tuesday. I think that Tuesday was in 1927.
Hands off the boiler jacket. She collects fingerprints and she is louder than I am.
One whistle is hello. That was four. Something down there is praying.
Cover your ears for the whistle. The warning was me, a minute ago. You missed it.
Pressure's normal. It's just that normal for this boiler is closer to 'imminent.'
The gauge says high. Oh, wrong gauge. That's my blood pressure.
Anyone here speak boiler? ... Then we are all promoted. She hisses when she's right.
Pressure's up. That's her voting. The vote is not for me.
We prefer to call it a 'dynamic water feature.'
The deck is wet by design. We call it a splash zone. The zone is the whole boat.
Madam, your shoes have gone over to the river. They're the first of us to arrive.
If you feel something wet, that's the river. If it feels like several, those are its friends.
Forecast. Sun on the bank, cloud on the ridge, rain in the boat.
Forecast says sunny. The forecast has never been in this boat.
That creak is structural. The boat is telling us a story. It's a long one, and it ends abruptly.
Listen. That's the hull. She's been through a lot, and she'd like to share.
Dent from '09. The dent beside it is from telling people about the dent from '09.
If a rivet lands in your lap, take it as a compliment. She's never given me one.
We patched it with a postcard from Cra-Zi. It's holding. It says 'Wish you were here.'
That patch is a postcard. It says 'Greetings from Cra-Zi.' I can't promise the greeting is mutual.
Seventeen bends to the mill. I counted. The river counted something else and didn't send the notes.
Seventeen bends between here and the mill. I asked the river why. It said 'scenery.'
Current's three knots. Which way, nobody's said. We assume downstream, out of politeness.
The current's gentle today. It's got somewhere to be and it's being polite about it.
Why is it that colour? ... Correct. Next.
That's not mud. That's sediment with a past.
Under us: catfish, eels, one philosopher, and a hat from the bend we just did.
If a fish looks at you, look back. If it waves, that's my department.
Mist on the water. Nature's way of saying 'don't ask me either.'
Mist is just fog that hasn't committed.
The chart was drawn by one man in one afternoon. He was very sure. It's the best thing about him.
He drew this in one sitting. That wasn't surprising as he didn't have a leg to stand on.
There's an X. I'm not stopping. Last X was a stump, and the stump had already had visitors.
X marks the spot. I'd tell you which spot, but nobody's come back to say.
The chart has a legend. It says 'Trust me.'
There's a legend in the corner of the chart. It's a single word, and the word is 'probably.'
Scale: One inch to the mile. *Turns the wheel hard* That doesn't measure up.
I measured the river against the scale. The river won.
Blank on the chart. We went. Write down mud.
Anyone want to fill in the blank? Pencil down. The last man who tried is the reason the blank is still there.
Do not wake them. Do not point. Do not breathe like a menu.
Four tons, eyes shut. The eyelids are the only part of this that is optional.
Sir. That yawn was not aimed at you. Sit, before it adjusts.
A hundred and fifty degrees of good morning.
Are they looking at us? ... They're looking at Ginny. Ginny is looking at me. I am looking at the timetable.
Hippos aren't aggressive. They're just very sure of themselves, and very large.
We name them. They don't come when called. Neither do I, in fairness.
This is Margaret. That's Dennis. Dennis is the one looking at you.
Elbows in, hats in laps. If it's tight, breathe out. If it's very tight, breathe out harder.
You. Widest shoulders aboard. Turn sideways. Everyone else, turn into him and think thin.
The cut has a marvellous echo. Go on. Say something kind to the river.
Listen to that echo. It's the only thing on the river that agrees with me.
Those walls are covered in the names of skippers who stood right here. Most of them in the past tense.
Carved in the rock: the name of everyone who's come through here. It's a long list. It's still on page one.
The Calliope. She chose that mud in 1913 and has not taken a counter-offer.
Don't hail her. She'll think we're the tide, and the tide has been a disappointment.
We pass. She stays. It's a friendship with one oar in it.
Anyone related to her skipper? ... No? She's been asking since the war. Wave anyway.
They say she's haunted. The ghost is very polite. It just keeps asking where the exit is.
Locals say she's haunted by the first skipper. He isn't angry. He just doesn't know the way out either.
The only thing coming out of that mine these days is the occasional sigh.
Closed years ago. They found everything in it. Then they found nothing. Then the bank found them.
They used to send a canary in first. These days it's a passenger. Don't worry. I'm joking. Mostly. Sit still.
Old miners sent a canary ahead. I've considered the same system with passengers. Sit still; I'm only considering.
A dead end. It's the nicest way I've found to describe my career.
Dead end. It has a certain charm, if you like a cul-de-sac with a hole in it.
Far bank's out there. ... There. Or there. We'll enter it as 'present' and keep going.
No snags, no walls, no excuses. I distrust a stretch with this much room.
Enjoy the calm. It's the calm they warn you about.
Smooth water. I'm told it's soothing. I find it suspicious.
Hands inside. The timber takes souvenirs and it does not run a stall.
Sign says Keep Out. Which is exactly what I told the water. Grab your buckets ladies and gents.
Ancient, hollow and utterly uninterested in your opinion of it. That's the timber, not the skipper. Though now you mention it.
These trees fell in a flood nobody wrote down. They haven't forgiven the river, and they've told it so.
Hats off the head and into the hand. Branches collect anything with a brim.
Madam, the brim is about to enlist. Hold it like you paid for it.
Full of teeth, says the margin. I've had dinner with the man who wrote the margin.
How many teeth in that one? ... The accepted answer on this boat is 'enough.'
The word is crocodile. If alligator comes out, follow it with an apology and a smaller word.
Long snout. That smile. He heard the other name. He is deciding what to do with it.
Let's scoot along. Now. Before the crocs come and tip the scales.
The mill quit in '04. The race did not get the letter.
Hold on. This water has an appointment, and we are standing in the hallway.
Down by the old mill stream. Lovely. Wrong water. This one does not own a stream.
The wheel's gone. The current stayed on. Typical staff.
It's tradition to leave an offering. Mine is an apology. It's been a long season.
Folks leave flowers. I leave a short note: 'Sorry about earlier.' It's a very general note.
Patron saint of misplaced things. Our papers have been devout since March.
Lost on this run: an oar, a hat, one surveyor. The shrine is undefeated.
Cameras up. If the saint comes out blurry, that was on purpose. Leave a coin anyway.
You, with the good camera. One of me looking as if I meant to be here.
Knight Falls. Named for a knight who went over. We don't say which way.
Named for Sir Reginald Knight, who was told 'don't' and was therefore never seen again.
Smell that? Flowers, that's the falls. Hot iron, that's the boiler. Fish, that's the passenger by the rail.
Mouths shut for the spray. The falls are not a pump and you are not a cup.
They call it mighty. I've never been sure who they asked.
Nine feet of water falling 108 inches. That's the advertised miracle, measured twice.
Nine feet. That's the drop, the poster, and the entire speech.
Anyone who has already fallen nine feet, keep the hand down. I don't want a competition.
Two in front, one behind. That's formation flying. Or a very small queue.
Look at them go. Not a bird among them knows where we're going, and yet they're ahead of us.
That's a goose. Ask it yourself. It'll give you an answer. At length.
The goose has opinions on the river, the boat and you. I'd leave it be.
Left or right. Both are wrong. One is less wrong, and I won't say which.
Left or right? I've done both. I'm told it's good to be consistent, so I've done both.
Nowhere is lovely this time of year. It's lovely every time of year. It's the one consistent thing about it.
The weather in Nowhere is always fine, because nobody has stayed long enough to complain.
There's a sign: 'Welcome to Nowhere.' Underneath it is another sign: 'Welcome Back.'
They built a monument to Nowhere. It's very modest. You'll walk past it and not notice. That's the point.
Next landing is Nowhere. Miss it and you're somewhere, and somewhere charges extra.
Who's getting off? ... All of you, in the long run. Not at this bell.
He's out of tune. The piano, I mean. The man in the boat is fine.
That's a very fine upright. The note you just heard is how it says hello to the river.
The ice is doing its best. The sun is doing its best. Neither is on our side.
It's a block of ice with ambitions. They're mostly in the form of puddles.
The leopard isn't scary. He's misunderstood. And bigger than the sign.
He's a very calm cat. He's also a very large cat. I'd treat those as separate facts.
Mail sacks. Seventeen letters of love, nine of complaint, and one that just says 'ha.'
Somewhere in those sacks is a love letter that will never arrive. I like to think the river's reading it.
Neither rain nor sleet nor hippos shall keep these sacks from being slightly damp.
The mail goes through. It goes through the river, mostly. Some of it arrives.
Eyes front through the market. A look is a deposit.
For sale off the port side: hats, maps, smoked fish, and a boat with fewer stories than this one.
Offer him half. If he laughs, you're close. If he cries, you're in the right market.
The price moves when you look at it. Look at the melon, not the number.
Little clay Ginny. Leaks in the same places. Doesn't float. I'd call that honest work.
Sir, if you buy the model, don't hold it up next to the original. One of them will take it badly.
Umbrellas, on a river. He's sold four. Two of those were to me. I won't discuss the weather.
No eye contact with the map roll. His river is straight. I will not be hearing about it.
Fog. Don't worry, I know the river. By ear. Mostly my ear, occasionally the boat's.
Lovely fog. You can't see a thing, which makes me an excellent skipper. I see no problems.
Horn. ... Listen. If something answers, we have company. If nothing answers, keep the company to yourself.
The horn says we are here. It has no opinion on where here is.
Shapes. Tree. Tree. Closer tree. I will tell you if we meet a fourth category.
You saw a face. I saw a buoy. The buoy gets the vote. Sit.
The chart says clear. The chart is in my coat. My coat has never been fog.
Dead reckoning. Put the stress on reckoning. The other word can stay in the book.
Seven feet of bridge. Eight of Ginny. I have written the bridge a letter.
Down before the end of this sentence.
This bridge is called Napoleon. Not for the emperor. For the clearance.
They named it James the Lesser. The greater one would not have fit.
Down. Lower. A little lower. ... That's the bridge's opinion of your posture.
You. The tall one. You are the demonstration. The rest of you, study him.
Anyone carrying a shilling for the toll? Keep it. The jar retired. We pay by slowing down.
One shilling, last collected in the war. The jar is still out. Ambition is free.
Teeth together. The river is about to play the cups, the chart, and your fillings.
Rattle order: tins, lantern, my nerve, your aunt's brooch. Brooch wins.
The rocks started it. The river is finishing the argument. We are the audience.
Who was having a quiet morning? ... Good. Hand it aft. We're done with it.
Hold the rail. The rail has a future. I am using both hands for the wheel.
Madam, take the child. Child, take the bench. Nobody take the wheel.
Lunch will be served downstream. Breakfast may join it.
Look at the horizon. Don't look at me. I am not a horizon and I am not well.
He has waved at every boat since 1898. This one counts. Don't make him do a second take.
Wave. He's paid by the boat, not by the friendship. We can still be accurate.
Stock of the island: one tree, one man, one opinion about boats.
Tallest tree on the island. Also the shortest. He has never lost an argument.
On three. One, two... he's early. We look like the late boat. Wave anyway.
Has he ever missed a boat? Once. Fog. He waved at the fog until it left.
They say the man on the island knows the secret of the river. I asked. He waved. I took it as a yes.
Sometimes I think he's the only one who knows where the river ends. He just waves. I think that's an answer.
The cable is his road. We are not on his road. We are briefly in his way.
Quiet on the wire. It sits at throat height and it does not make conversation.
Duck. Now. The other now.
Centre bench, tall hat. You and that wire are about to be introduced. Remove the hat.
His route is from this bank to this bank. Fully booked, all season.
Waiting since Tuesday. Tuesday got off and walked. He's still timing her.
She's at full steam. That's not a warning. That's an ambition.
The gauge is in the red. It isn't alarming; it's committed.
If she bangs, that is the boiler saying her name. Clap later.
Hands off the steam pipes. They've been working all day, and they bite.
Our speed this morning is imminent.
Anyone actually in a hurry? ... The boiler is. Sit back and let her have it.
We're not sinking. We're descending, with dignity.
The water is at the rail. I'm told that's good for morale. It isn't. But I'm told.
Buckets under the bench. The river came aboard without a ticket. Show it the side.
That gurgle is water, sitting where a floorboard used to have the only say.
You are sitting in the new attraction. We call it the indoor river. Mind the brochure.
Sir, your socks have changed sides. Bail from where you are and we'll discuss terms.
Something just left the boat. It was not on the manifest and it did not say goodbye.
Piece in your hand? Hold it up. I'll tell you whether we needed it or whether it needed us.
Hear that? Say hello back, then sit as if the hull can see you.
The structure would like a word. The word was that crack.
What's holding: paint, a lashing, and a theory I will explain in Nowhere.
Hands off the paint. The paint has seniority and a short temper.
Count the problems with me. One. Two. Three. Stop. After three it's a hobby, and hobbies are extra.
Don't panic. I'll do the panicking. It's my first day.
Fire above, river below, and both of them on the timetable.
Is this part of the fare? ... It is. So is the bucket by your foot.
Questions at the end, please. Buckets at the beginning.
The show goes on. Tonight the show is the bilge, and the bilge is a professional.
Don't wave at them. They wave back, and there are more of them than polite.
Orange. Every one. Nobody on the bank approved it. Here they are anyway.
Three weeks of life, and they're spending the afternoon on Ginny. I'm flattered. I'm also in the lane.
Are we stopped? ... No. They are. It's a lunch. We'll go around the lunch.
One on your shoulder stays. Two is a meeting, and you don't have the chair.
No clapping. They are not an act. They are traffic with better colour.
Kettle Rocks. Nature's tea service. Guests are advised not to be the tea.
Tea, anyone? ... She's been ready since before the town. We are not pulling in for a cup.
Nobody has ever made tea on those rocks. They remember.
Stay clear of the steam. Those rocks have been boiling since before kettles. They're not stopping for tea.
Two kettles on this river. One is geology. Ours is under your boots and she is proud.
Do not praise the spring where the boiler can hear it. She keeps score.
Eleven. All facing the boat. Nobody fishing. I think we've been found guilty.
Which one's the foreman? ... The one with the dry beak. That's none of them. We're free. Probably.
Beak bigger than the belly. Also bigger than the hat you are about to drop.
Fits in there: a fish, a glove, and the last clean order I gave.
Eyes on the tall one. When he goes, you go quiet. He has a plan.
He hits like a gavel. Court is open. We are not the plaintiff.
I am saluting that flag. The flag is a pair of trousers. Carry on.
Whose line is that? Don't tell me. If you know, you're late for the washing.
Heads down. Sheets incoming. They are wider than Ginny and cleaner than anyone aboard.
You in the white shirt. Stay low or the line will hire you.
Monday on the left, Sunday on the right. We are sailing through Thursday. Mind the collar.
Look along the line, not into it. A clothesline is not a window and Thursday is not your business.
Nine hundred years of bowing. I want the name of the skipper who told him to start.
What is he sorry for? Hands down. We will miss the bend if we open the list.
Bow with me. Luck is not in the fare. The statue is, and he keeps a book.
Eleven years I've bowed at this bend. The luck has been very punctual about not arriving.
A hundred feet of stone. No oar, no rope, no interest in our departure time.
If he ever stepped off, we'd have a new channel. He has declined. I respect it.
Paper lanterns so the boats can be seen. Also so the boats can be discussed. Wave like you heard neither.
Leave them on the string. They're for the boats that come back, and I'd like to be one.
The whole bank is out. Wave as if we are the boat they stayed up for.
Waving or warning? ... Wave. We'll read the minutes downstream.
For six minutes the river looks as if it costs money. Don't tell it.
I'd buy one of those moons. I have nowhere to hang it but the boiler, and she would talk.
No pointing. Pointing is for snags. This is a show, and the cast has already seen you.
No ticket, wet ushers, no interval. Best house on the run.
Down the mud. No chart, no meeting, no second thought. I am trying not to applaud.
Who's having a go? ... The otters vote no. I vote no. The mud abstains.
They'll go again. There. Told you. That's the whole natural history.
